articles.title: SC rules 24-hour arrest deadline begins from detention, not formal arrest
articles.summary:
The Supreme Court on Thursday ruled that the 24-hour constitutional deadline for producing an arrested person before a magistrate begins from the moment he is detained, and not from the time the police formally makes the arrest.
Holding that there can be no artificial distinction between 'arrest' and 'detention' for the purpose of Article 22(2) of the Constitution, a bench of Justices Ujjal Bhuyan and Atul S Chandurkar said any interpretation allowing the police to exclude the period of pre-arrest detention would be contrary to the constitutional mandate.
"The view that 24 hours begin only from the formal arrest is contrary to the constitutional mandate of Article 22(2) and Section 56 of the BNSS," the bench observed.
The verdict that the only period that can be excluded while computing the 24-hour deadline is the time reasonably required to travel from the place of arrest to the magistrate's court.

articles.title: Tata Motors, Ashok Leyland shares rocket up to 12%. Here are 2 reasons fuelling the sharp surge
articles.summary: Shares of commercial vehicle majors Ashok Leyland and Tata Motors rallied as much as 12% on Thursday after a sharp drop in oil prices, which boosted investor sentiment amid hopes of an Iran deal.In today’s session, Ashok Leyland shares rallied as much as 12% to Rs 172 on the BSE, while commercial vehicle major Tata Motors jumped 9% to Rs 440.Why are these 2 stocks rising?1.) Oil tumbles 10% in two days - Crude oil prices crashed over a percent on Thursday, extending losses from a 9% plunge in the previous session as markets assessed the implications of the Democrats' sweeping victory over Republicans in the US midterm elections.The political setback raised expectations that mounting pressure on the Republican Party could push the Trump administration toward ending the war with Iran through a negotiated settlement.Brent crude was trading at $93.51 a barrel, down more than 1%, or $1.05 in absolute terms. US West Texas Intermediate (WTI) crude slipped 1.35% to below $87 a barrel. In the previous session, Brent futures settled $8.98, or 8.7%, lower at $94.62 a barrel, while WTI crude futures dropped $7.97, or 8.3%, to $88.12. Both benchmarks ended Wednesday at their lowest levels since August 31.Falling crude oil prices are positive for commercial vehicle (CV) manufacturers such as Ashok Leyland and Tata Motors as diesel accounts for a significant portion of fleet operators' running costs. Lower fuel prices improve the operating economics of truck and bus owners, potentially encouraging fleet expansion, replacement demand and fresh vehicle purchases. Cheaper crude also reduces input and logistics costs for automakers, supporting margins. Additionally, lower fuel prices can ease inflationary pressures and improve overall economic activity, benefiting freight movement and transportation demand.2.) Buoyant market mood - The Indian stock market opened Thursday's session on a strong note, with benchmark indices Sensex and Nifty rallying nearly 2% amid a favourable mix of global and domestic cues. Gains by Democrats in the US midterm elections, marking a setback for US President Donald Trump, along with easing crude oil prices, boosted investor sentiment and extended Dalal Street's recovery rally for a second consecutive session.The Sensex surged over 1,400 points to cross the 78,700 mark, while the Nifty 50 jumped more than 400 points to reclaim 24,350. The sharp rally added nearly Rs 8 lakh crore to the combined market capitalisation of BSE-listed companies, taking it to Rs 501 lakh crore.Broader markets also participated in the rally, with the Nifty Midcap 100 and Nifty Smallcap 250 indices gaining up to 1.5%. Meanwhile, India VIX, the market's volatility gauge, declined 2.5% to slip below the 15 mark.Among sectoral indices, Nifty Auto, Nifty Financial Services and Nifty Realty emerged as major outperformers, rising more than 2% each.With tailwinds for the economy getting stronger, the bullish trend in the market is set to continue, said VK Vijayakumar, Chief Investment Strategist at Geojit Investments. He noted that the strongest positive for the market is the sharp 10% fall in Brent crude to around $94 level.This decline is in hopes that a resolution to the US-Iran conflict is likely soon since this conflict and the consequent high crude prices contributed significantly to the Republican rout in the midterms.Disclaimer: This article has been written by Veer Sharma, who is not a SEBI-registered Research Analyst or an Investment Adviser. articles.title: Trump’s pain makes D-Street bulls gain! IndiGo, Asian Paints, other crude-sensitive stocks rally up to 8% as oil drops below $95
articles.summary: Shares of paint makers, airlines, tyre manufacturers and oil marketing companies (OMCs) rallied up to 8% on Thursday as oil prices plunged nearly 10%, falling below $100 per barrel after weeks. The decline came amid a major setback for US President Donald Trump, whose Republican Party lost control of both houses of Congress in the midterm elections.Brent crude futures slipped below the $95-per-barrel mark to trade under $94, while WTI crude futures fell below $87 on Thursday morning.The sharp decline in crude prices lifted sentiment towards companies that use oil as a key raw material, as well as airlines that have been grappling with elevated aviation fuel costs. Investors also cheered the prospect of lower input costs for paint and tyre makers, while easing crude prices could offer relief to oil marketing companies.Crude-sensitive stocks rallyAmong the airlines, IndiGo shares surged 7% to trade at Rs 5,489 apiece, while SpiceJet shares jumped around 5%. Paint-maker Asian Paints saw its shares rally nearly 7%, while those of peers Indigo Paints and Berger Paints jumped up to 5%.MRF shares rallied more than 4%, with each share gaining Rs 4,995 to trade at Rs 1.23 lakh apiece. Apollo Tyres and Balkrishna Industries shares jumped more than 8%. Oil marketing companies, including Hindustan Petroleum Corporation (HPCL), Bharat Petroleum Corporation (BPCL) and Indian Oil Corporation (IOC) saw their share prices jump up to 7%.Also read | Why is Dalal Street rallying today?Why are oil prices falling today?US President Donald Trump’s Republican party lost control over both the houses of Congress, the Senate and House of Representatives. This came after the US-Iran war spiked energy prices, with Americans beginning to feel the pinch in their pockets. In a lengthy post after the party’s election defeat, Vice President JD Vance acknowledged voter dissatisfaction over the war. He said this, along with rising cost of living and other factors may have led to voters’ dissatisfaction, which in turn led to Democrats’ sweeping victory in the midterm elections.One of the things the data analysts on our side obsessed over was "composition"—whether the electorate looked close enough to 2024 for Republicans to win. And despite polls that showed a Democrat blowout, the data kept on telling us the same story: in some states turnout was merely OK, in other states it was downright amazing, and in no state was it catastrophic. There was a genuine sense of optimism on our team: our people were showing up. So, I asked the smartest data guy I know, does that mean we're going to shock the world? "No," he told me. "We might do better than the polls suggest. But the data is telling us that a lot of Trump/Vance 2024 voters are pissed and planning to vote for the other guys. Our voters are turning out, but they may not vote for us."Well, that looks prophetic now. Our voters did show up. In Florida, for example, the electorate was 9 points more Republican than Democrat, just a couple points worse than 2024. Undoubtedly there were places we could have done better on turnout. But the main problem is not turnout. The main problem is that many people who voted for Trump/Vance in 2024 voted for Democrats in 2026.  There will be a lot of infighting and arguing over what happened and why that is. One of the pollsters I really respect told me that our economic messaging wasn’t sharp enough down the stretch. I’m sure that’s true. But the real reason we lost is obvious to almost everyone. Another pollster—one of the smartest people I know in politics, told me yesterday we’d lose the generic ballot by 13 points. I felt negative going into Tuesday, but even I was shocked by this. In his polling, he saw that a lot of Trump 2024 voters were angry and planning to vote for Democrats. He asked those voters who had abandoned us what would cause them to come back on our team. The top four answers, accounting for nearly all of the responses were:1) End the war2) Focus on cost of living/inflation3) Put America First4) Change our relationship to IsraelOur voters showed up. And the above four reasons are why many of them voted for Democrats. This is according to a pollster who nailed the results. While many spent Monday attacking Rachel Campos Duffy for calling for a diplomatic resolution to the conflict, it turns out her political advice was sound. (She’s also a great person.)In the next few months, there's going to be a lot of gaslighting. Expect to hear any number of establishment politicians say the solution to our woes is amnesty. I'm open to the idea that we should change enforcement—by focusing more on businesses that hire illegal labor, for instance. But anyone pushing amnesty is lying to you. The reason we lost is the war. The president himself said so last night. If you'd like to argue it was worth it, that losing the Senate for the next 6 years was worth it, then do so. Argue it was a worthwhile cost to pay. Agree or disagree, that's at least honest.But everyone knows why we lost. And any honest conversation about where we go from here must start there.I remain hopeful about our country. To the people who are pissed off and want to say, “I told you so”: you’re right, you did tell us so. Take that energy into electing Republicans who share your worldview. To the people who are just pissed at the results, you should be. Let’s take that anger and get back to the work of saving our country.— JD Vance (@JDVance) November 4, 2026Senate Minority Leader Chuck Schumer, a Democrat, meanwhile pledged to bring the war to an end soon. “We are going to end the war," he said at a news conference in Washington. "We have some Republicans already who have joined us in ending the war, and the Founding Fathers had the power of the purse as one of the ways of deterring a president who does war without the consent of the American people,” he said.This retriggered hopes for a conclusion to the Middle East conflict that has been raging since late February this year following US and Israel’s joint military strikes on Iran, killing its former supreme leader, triggering a massive surge in oil prices and rattling global stock markets.As a result, oil prices tumbled. "Markets are assessing the impact of the midterm elections to Donald Trump's next steps with the Iran war, pricing in more likelihood for the war to end," Reuters quoted June Goh, senior oil analyst at Sparta Commodities.Also read | Oil Price Today (November 5): Crude oil falls below $94 after 9% plunge on Wednesday after midterm results. More downside ahead?What lies ahead for crude sensitive stocks?With majority in both the houses with the Democrats, war-related spending approvals are likely to be trimmed and may ease off crude oil supply related challenges through the Strait of Hormuz, said  Sunny Agrawal, Head of Fundamental Research at SBI Securities. He noted that in case crude oil prices sustains below $90-100 per barrel, then the entire inflationary narrative will take back seat and this augurs well for the Indian economy and equity markets.“We believe the crude or crude derivatives and interest rate sensitive sectors are likely to be the key beneficiaries in the short to medium term. With likely recovery in rupee, FII inflows should accelerate and should be positive for large and midcaps,” the analyst further said.Disclaimer: This article has been written by Debaroti Adhikary, who is not a SEBI-registered Research Analyst or an Investment Adviser. articles.title: The midterm verdict on Trump's economy
articles.summary: Washington: President Donald Trump was publicly humbled by inflation in Tuesday's midterm elections, as rising prices provoked a blistering set of losses for Republicans in House, Senate and gubernatorial races.Most voters said that Trump's own policies had smothered growth and drove costs even higher, according to The AP Voter Poll, a survey of roughly 100,000 midterm voters.Also Read: Democrats vow bill to end Iran war after midterm sweepThe president's message that the fault lay with his predecessor, Democrat Joe Biden, didn't land. Americans saw prices start to climb with Trump's chaotic rash of tariffs last year, and energy costs spiked after he launched a war with Iran in February.About two-thirds of voters said Trump's own policies had fueled inflation. By contrast, only about half of 2022 midterm voters said this about Biden's policies, according to AP VoteCast.Voters in states from California to Mississippi were broadly in agreement that Trump's taxes on foreign imports have done more harm than good.The election results matched what voters had been telling pollsters for months, but Trump had campaigned with a decidedly deaf ear."I've done a great job," Trump said at one of his final midterm rallies in Iowa. "Prices are coming way down."Voters have buyer's remorse with TrumpDemocratic victories in Tuesday's midterms signaled that most voters don't believe the economy or Trump is working for them.Consumer prices are up 3.7% over the past 12 months, compared to an inflation rate of 3% when Trump began his second term. The president told reporters on Wednesday that the Iran war "drove the gasoline up a little bit short-term," but he felt the choice to fight Iran was worth it because of its push for nuclear weapons. "If I had to do it again, I'd have to do it again," he said.There is no guarantee that a House and Senate with a Democratic majority can fix an economy pestered by uncomfortably high inflation. Trump and Congress would likely need to work on a bipartisan basis, or simply keep the economy stable enough to allow the Federal Reserve to ratchet down inflation through its setting of interest rates.But voters did prefer Democrats to the status quo of a president who could govern with little to no congressional pushback from Republicans.About 9 in 10 voters said the cost of living was a "crucial" or "major" factor in their vote for Congress. And about 6 in 10 of this group backed Democratic candidates in their local House races.The economy is still growing, but AI is a source of fear instead of hopeThe underlying economy is stronger than many Americans think, with the S&P 500 stock index up more than 10% so far this year and the unemployment rate at a healthy 4.2%. Investors greeted the news of Democratic wins as a positive with stocks up on Wednesday.Still, the major driver of growth has been the buildout of artificial intelligence - a boom that Trump has actively stoked by refusing to codify more aggressive federal oversight.Voters don't share Trump's optimism about AI, which he has renamed "super intelligence" in federal documents.Instead of buying the arguments that AI would increase productivity and accelerate growth, about 6 in 10 voters said AI will do more to hurt society.The technology could displace workers as jobs get automated or it could be a financial bubble that if popped could wreak havoc on retirement savings. Despite the anxiety, only about one-quarter of voters said AI was a "crucial" factor.Wealth isn't trickling down to the middle classTech billionaires such as Meta's Mark Zuckerberg, Nvidia's Jensen Huang and Elon Musk have become frequent guests of Trump, attending state dinners or jetting aboard with the president. But the growing concentration of wealth has been disconcerting for voters.Nationwide, about 7 in 10 voters said the economy favors the wealthy, while only about 3 in 10 said it's fair to everyday Americans. The wealth gap has become so extreme that even a majority of voters with a 2025 household income of $300,000 or more in the tech-heavy state of California felt the economy was tilted toward the rich.Still, a slight majority of voters across the country had a "somewhat" or "very" favorable impression of capitalism, compared to about one-third who "strongly" or "somewhat" favor socialism.But the election suggested that voters believe the government should use its heft to help reduce the cost of healthcare. About 6 in 10 said they wanted the government to play a "bigger role" in addressing medical expenses. Most voters said Trump's policies have made healthcare costs worse.Trump caught in a trap with votersHow voters felt about the overall economy generally depended on the size of their paychecks. While Trump campaigned on stats suggesting record low poverty, the working poor saw their own finances as crumbling.For those earning less than $50,000 a year, about 6 in 10 said they were worse off now than they were two years ago before Trump became president.People with higher incomes felt better about the economy, but that created a different problem for Trump. Higher-income voters were more concerned about the state of American democracy, and voters focused on democracy overwhelmingly broke for Democrats. Without congressional approval, Trump laid off thousands of federal workers, altered federal spending and imposed hundreds of billions of dollars in new tariffs that the Supreme Court earlier this year ruled were illegal.About 4 in 10 households with 2025 household incomes above $200,000 said that democracy was their top issue, putting the issue about even with the economy. Voters in most lower-income categories, on the other hand, clearly prioritized the economy.Overall, a slim majority of voters said government corruption was a crucial factor for their vote, while about half said this about high prices. Right now, nothing Trump offers comes with a guarantee that it will last beyond January 2029," Bosack told AFP, referring to the date when the US president's second term ends.Kim's deepening ties with Russia and China have also strengthened his position and reduced his incentive to engage with Washington.North Korea's economy grew more than three percent for a third straight year in 2025, Seoul's central bank estimated in July, citing Pyongyang's "expansion of economic cooperation with Russia" as its major driver.Nuclear ambitionsEven if Trump and Kim agree to meet, their differences over North Korea's nuclear weapons programme remain a major obstacle to any breakthrough.Pyongyang has repeatedly made clear it is no longer prepared to discuss denuclearisation.Kim Yo Jong said in September that the country's nuclear-armed status was "absolute", calling those hoping for denuclearisation "idiots".It came as South Korea's dovish President Lee Jae Myung -- who has repeatedly offered Pyongyang talks without preconditions -- suggested Washington seek a freeze, rather than the immediate elimination, of the North's nuclear programme and offer sanctions relief in return.That approach would face significant obstacles following Trump's midterm defeat though, with Democrats committed to denuclearisation and Congress holding powers over sanctions relief."Pyongyang retains negative memories of failing to make progress in negotiations under the Biden administration because of its position that there would be no sanctions relief or dialogue without prior denuclearisation measures," Kyungnam University's Lim said.North Korea's distrust of Washington, coupled with the uncertainty surrounding any agreement with Trump, could boost its nuclear ambitions."North Korea's belief that independently advancing its nuclear arsenal, regardless of changes in US administrations or political parties, was the right and strategically sound decision will be further reinforced," Lim said.Pyongyang has carried out a flurry of weapons tests in recent weeks, including trials of cluster-bomb warheads, attack drones, a precision-guided torpedo system and an intermediate-range hypersonic missile."The development, testing and training of new weapons will become regular and routine activities," Lim predicted.

AI stocks retreat as Democratic sweep puts data centre boom in focus
articles.summary: Wall Street's rally following the Democratic sweep of Congress did not extend to several companies riding the AI boom. Data centre builders and related technology stocks fell on Wednesday as investors weighed the possibility of greater political scrutiny of the industry's rapid expansion, Bloomberg reports.CoreWeave, Iren and Nebius declined, while power equipment makers GE Vernova and Vertiv also came under pressure. Chipmakers Nvidia and Marvell Technology slipped even as the Nasdaq 100 rose more than 1%.For live updates on US Markets, click here The election has brought concerns about rising electricity bills and AI-driven job losses into sharper focus. Meanwhile, investors were already questioning whether the industry's debt-fuelled spending can be sustained. According to Bloomberg, analysts do not expect political pressure to derail AI development, it could slow the pace of data centre expansion and investment.Also Read: Democrats’ Senate win could shield Federal Reserve from Trump’s influence, but risks persist“The Democrats will not in my opinion challenge what has already been implemented to win this race when it comes to AI. Because there is now a big competition between China and the US when it comes to technology,” Mabrouk Chetouane, Head of Global Market Strategy at Natixis Investment Managers, told Bloomberg.“Some of the questions on data centers suggested concerns about regulation should be faded, but others suggested they should remain in the spotlight. Regardless of what does or does not happen with Congress on this issue, risk does remain from the governors’ results as AI/data centers was a top issue in the close campaigns for those seats,” Lori Calvasina, Head of US Equity Strategy at RBC Capital Markets, said.“We still struggle to support the idea that the election will be a major clearing event for markets, however, given the absence of the usual turbulence in the US equity market around the election so far.”“This does add uncertainty about the path forward and maybe the pace forward, but ultimately we still think that the data center build-out will continue. Maybe the pace changes on the margin, but we ultimately think there’s huge demand for compute and that there may be some changes in how the data centers have to approach this, meaning maybe some of the tax incentives change, maybe some of the counties that really voted against this, maybe they have to move, go somewhere else. They might have to find other alternatives. But we think ultimately — much like fracking — we still expect that we see a buildout. It just may be done with some different concessions, with some guardrails, more guardrails than we had before,” Kieth Lerner, Chief Investment Officer and Chief Market Strategist at Truist Advisory Services, was quoted as saying by Bloomberg.“Republicans or Democrats sitting in any state around the country, not just Texas, look at a state that historically has been Republican friendly with a largely effective governor, seeing them overthrown on this basis that data centers are an unpopular position. I think politicians, if anything, love to get reelected before they think about policy. And so more and more, whether it be Republican or Democrat, are likely to jump on that bandwagon to air quotes protect their state from data centers. Obviously that is a popular narrative,” Brad Long, Chief Investment Officer at Wealthspire, said.“It’s certainly not going to change the fact that data centers will be built out and there’s a lot of demand and there’s a lot of backlog. The question will be the regulation and the time and the throughput there. What markets are going to have to digest is, it’s not will data centers be built, but where and how long will it take and how much red tape will be there? Which obviously pushes further out not just all the capex spending, but the throughput on the benefit from AI,” said Matt Maley, Chief Market Strategist at Miller Tabak + Co.“The headwinds are getting a little bit bigger for the AI movement. That’s going to give us some tough sledding. So it may be a lot harder for the market to see the usual year-end rally in the midterm election years. The ‘not in my backyard’ with data centers is gonna be a 2028 issue immediately, and I think that the 2028 campaign starts today. ... It is all but impossible for the Republicans to win the presidency or win the Electoral College without winning Texas,” he added.“Narrative-wise, I think the initial ‘Glass Half-Full’ post ‘Blue Tsunami’ midterm Elections -trade is based upon the following rationalizations—some probably obvious, some more nuanced: A belief that the election results will lead to a forced moderation of US datacenter buildout, which then calms concerns around the Hyperscaler Capex race-to-infinity ‘prisoner’s dilemma’…Which from a markets-perspective reduces some of financing concerns around magnitude of credit and equities issuance, slows the “FCF burn” -trajectory fears,” said Charlie McElligott, Cross Asset Strategist at Nomura Holdings Inc.“There’s definitely some fears about what this might mean for the AI build-out, especially on data centers, and those names have already been under pressure because of the expected Democratic victory. But I think it’s probably a little bit overblown. It’s going to put more onus on the states, but I don’t think that that will impact existing projects all that much. But it could result in higher cost of production if these companies have to provide maybe more local assistance or navigate more regulation across the board just to get some of these projects through. But we still need these data centers,” JP Powers, Chief Investment Officer at RWA Wealth Partners, told Bloomberg.“You could read this as a vote against data centers, but at some level there’s a lot of momentum toward building them, there’s a lot of jobs at stake. The boulder’s already rolling down the hill to some extent, so the election of a few governors and a change in Congress is not going to completely stop the momentum,” Steve Sosnick, Chief Strategist at Interactive Brokers, said.“The market’s been expressing very valid fears that the money is just being spent too aggressively and that the borrowing is so extreme. And so maybe this slows it down to something that’s a bit more manageable, which isn’t great for the suppliers, but may actually impose a little financial discipline on the industry that markets are okay with.”“This is a wake up call. They have to really get out and make their case why communities should want data centers. I think in the end they will be successful, but it probably slows some of these projects down,” Peter Tchir, Head of Macro Strategy at Academy Securities, said.“Gov-elect Hinojosa favors an immediate moratorium on data center builds in Texas until new laws can be passed to establish guardrails. One interpretation is that existing builds / permits would be free to continue and all new construction would be halted and thus would move to other states. Another interpretation is that the datacenter build is slowing and likely reducing capex; this theme had been building into the election,” Andrew Tyler, Head of Global Market Intelligence at JPMorgan Chase & Co., told Bloomberg. “We would not abandon the Tech trade and would play for a tactical rebound, but we may see the market become increasingly selective of Tech / AI winners and losers.” (Disclaimer: This article is based on inputs from agencies. These do not represent the views of The Economic Times)

articles.summary: New Delhi: Oil prices may remain elevated as President Donald Trump's weakened political position after the midterms complicates efforts to end the Iran war and Tehran grows more emboldened, industry executives said, although crude oil cooled hours after the results came out.Brent futures dropped $9.27, or 8.9%, to $94.29 a barrel, touching the lowest level since September 4. US West Texas Intermediate crude futures were down $7.44, or 7.8%, to $88.54.Also read: And quiet flows the Don: Trump goes from rage to rapproachementTrump could seek to demonstrate strength by intensifying military operations against Iran, but Democrats' control of Congress could constrain his ability to fund the war in West Asia. "Trump has already lost the midterms and cannot seek re-election. To prove the American public that he is right, he may escalate the military conflict," an executive said.Since the war began, Trump has pursued two objectives: intensifying military pressure on Iran while keeping oil prices in check, often by signalling that the conflict was nearing an end and would not escalate. With the elections behind him, he may be more willing to let oil prices rise in the short term and focus on achieving his military objectives.A decisive outcome, whether through military action or a deal, would be preferable to the prolonged stalemate that has imposed heavy costs on oil importers, executives said. But an escalation involving ground forces could also prolong the conflict, further disrupting energy supplies and raising costs for consumers.A deal with Iran could offer Trump a way to claim victory while bringing down oil prices and easing the cost-of-living pressures that contributed to the Republicans' defeat. However, a settlement that allows Iran to impose a permanent toll on shipping through Hormuz could undermine Trump's ambition to be remembered as one of America's greatest presidents, another executive said.Also read: Trump admits Iran war hurt Republicans in midterms but says ‘Iran thing’ had to be doneIndian refiners would ideally prefer unrestricted passage through Hormuz, an executive said.Whether or not Iran is allowed to levy a toll, a resolution that restores the flow of oil through the strait would reduce the risk premium on crude prices and bring down freight rates, lowering procurement costs for importers such as India, he said.Brent crude is near $100 a barrel, while freight and insurance costs are several times higher than before the war. Brent was around $70 before the war started.The cost of the prolonged disruption has been compounded by uncertainty over the reliability of supplies. Although oil flows through the strait have risen sharply in the past two months, they remain expensive and unpredictable, making the current situation unsustainable for importers."This is better than no flows at all but definitely not sustainable," an executive said.

articles.title: Don Trump goes from rage to rapproachement
articles.summary: TOI Correspondent From Washington: The man who posts on social media at the drop of a hat, at all times and at odd hours, sometimes a dozen posts an hour, was rendered rather speechless after an electoral thrashing for the ages.Now a lame-duck President for all purposes but still armed with enormous executive powers, Donald Trump reacted to the Republican rout first with a mix of denial and defiance, and later with nonchalance and some conciliation. His initial reaction when the Democratic demolistion came into view early on Tuesday night was one of denial. “I wasn’t on the Ballot and if I was, we would have won IN A LANDSLIDE!” he posted on his propaganda platform “Truth Social.”Track US Senate Elections Result 2026 Live Updates hereThen it was a couple of rage posts about Fox News -- his favored propaganda network whose coverage became funereal as the night wore on -- and blaming Republican candidates, including defeated Texas Governor Greg Abbott, a wheelchair-bound GOP stalwart who was thwarted in his bid for a third term.“If Greg Abbott hadn’t become a RINO (Republican in Name Only) in the last six months of his Political Life, he wouldn’t have lost. He went back to his original formula, and it wasn’t pretty!” he wrote, throwing the veteran under the bus and absolving himself of all blame. He told Fox News that some voters simply “didn’t like the candidates.”Shortly after midnight, he posted a photo of a red baseball cap with the word VETO on it – suggesting that he will simply block any Democrat-written bills, creating a deadlock since Dems do not have the 2/3rds majority in both chambers to override a presidential veto.Then he went silent for more than nine hours, but not before he also told a C-Span in a live phone call that he would work with Democrats and not veto everything they sent, even though he has the right to do so.Also read: US midterm elections 2026: Democrats sweep House and Senate, deal Trump major blow"We're going to work with the Democrats, to make sure things go well for our country... We have a lot of friends in the Democratic Party,” he said in a conciliatory tone at odds with his familiar combativeness.Democrats too have every reason to work with the President. The U.S Constitution (Article I, Section 7) requires a two-thirds majority vote in both the House of Representatives (290/435) and the Senate (67/100) to overcome the veto – although the qualifier is 2/3rds majority of those “present and voting." Dems are well short of that double which last occurred in 1965 during the Lyndon Johnson Presidency.But a testing time is afoot even within the Republican ranks. The rout shocked and angered many conservatives, some of whom began to turn on Trump publicly. “Dems look like they might get 56 (Senate seats).. Rs will never get that back for a long time. You ignore primaries for years, anoint a charlatan as not just leader but God, and then mimic his retardation every day for a decade, at some point the chickens come home to roost,” raged Daniel Horowitz, a commentator at the right leaning outlet The Blaze. "It's on him. It's not on anybody else. It's a total, complete rejection of President Trump," Bill Miller, a top Republican lobbyist in Texas, told BBC, calling it “a disaster of the first magnitude” that nobody saw coming.Also read: US Vice President JD Vance says Iran war is 'the reason we lost' midterms 2026Actually, every poll and survey other than MAGA affiliated ones saw it coming, although the scale was not foreseen by most. In fact, Democrats went to polling day wary of the “too good to be true” projections given past setbacks, particularly in 2016 when Trump himself did not appear to believe he would win. This time around, he tried to conjure up victory in the face of imminent defeat with bravado and bluster, but voters had other ideas. They trussed him up by giving Democrats a comfortable majority in both chambers of Congress.

Iran has exempted commercial ships from four countries, including India and China, from transit restrictions in the Strait of Hormuz, a top Iranian official has said, amid continued attacks on vessels attempting to cross the strategic waterway.

articles.title: Aswath Damodaran trims his Anthropic IPO valuation to $1.45 trillion; Dean of valuation explains why
articles.summary: Valuation expert Aswath Damodaran trimmed his valuation estimate for AI giant Anthropic to $1.45 trillion, from his earlier estimate of $1.475 trillion which was already lower than the industry estimates of $2 trillion.The 'Dean of Valuation' in a long blogpost said his earlier valuation estimate which was lower than the overall market view received strong reactions. Some of them were solely based on emotion, he said, as they held strong conviction in the company. Some of it was based on cost of capital, which the analyst believes reflects a fundamental disconnect with market history, current market pricing and basic business sense.Also read | Dean of valuation Aswath Damodaran pegs Anthropic's worth at $1.475 trillion ahead of mega IPOHis latest $1.45 trillion valuation accounts for the trailing 12-month revenue and operating income numbers to include the just-leaked third quarter numbers. “The equity value that I obtain for Anthropic is close to the lower end of the offering price estimates, but as I noted at the time that I posted it, and will reinforce again now, it is a function of not just my upbeat story about the company, but also one about how the AI products and services market will evolve over time,” he wrote.Aswath Damodaran’s worries for AnthropicDamodaran estimates Anthropic’s target revenues will reach a trillion dollars in ten years. Not only would this put them at or close to the top of all companies, in terms of total annual revenues, but they will also be sharing that grouping with companies like Amazon and Walmart that deliver on scale, but at the expense of margins, he said, adding that Anthropic emerges as a winner in the premium portion of the AI market, capturing a dominant market share, with pricing power.In his previous post valuing Anthropic, Damodaran had raised the alarm over the company’s governance structure, stating that its structure as a public benefit corporation and a voting share concoction that leaves founders in control, no matter how much capital the company raises in equity markets. He said he received feedback that this may not be a negative as these are smart people who know AI better than the rest. The analyst is however not convinced as he believes concentration of power in the hands of founders is a bad idea.Also read | Aswath Damodaran explains why country risk is no longer just an emerging market problem“While much of the focus on Anthropic has been on their compute commitments, disclosed (loosely) in their prospectus, my valuation of Anthropic is driven by expectations of what those commitments will look like over time, and especially if my growth story for the company comes into fruition. Delivering a trillion dollars of revenues will require Anthropic to not just maintain and replenish the compute power that it has already locked down, but add to that power over time,” Damodaran said, warning that building new data centers is getting more difficult, as local communities push back, and politicians realize that opposing them is a net vote winnerRegulatory risks are also one of the key worries for Anthropic. “Put simply, Anthropic will become riskier, if revenues do not measure up to expectations and the pathway to profitability becomes rockier, making it more an output than an input variable,” the valuation expert said.How investors should react to Anthropic’s IPO?While Damodaran remains cautious about Anthropic’s IPO, he noted that uncertainty is a feature of investing, no matter what one invests in, with the differences across investments lying in how much uncertainty one face, rather than whether she faces.Also read | AI boom heading for a dot-com-style bust? ‘Dean of Valuation’ Aswath Damodaran warns correction could be more painful than 2008He listed out four responses to such uncertainties.1) Ignore it: Damodaran pointed out that there are investors who are capable of ignoring uncertainty and going in fully even on the most uncertain investments. They are able to do so because they are far less risk averse than the rest and are willing to live with the consequences of investments (and their portfolios) blowing up. “They are more gamblers than investors, but with good instincts and timing, gamblers can get wealthy too,” he said.2) Avoid it: If an investor completely wants to avoid uncertainty, she cannot invest in equities, corporate bonds, which have risk of default, and even treasury bonds, which have price risk from shifting interest rates, Damodaran noted. Unless the investor simply wants to just hold cash, she has to therefore decide what her threshold for risk is, and stay within that threshold.3) Margin of Safety: The third approach to dealing with uncertainty also borrows from conventional value investing and imposing a margin of safety, where you will buy a stock only if its price is less than your value estimate by a margin (20%, 30%, 40%) that you specify.4) Law of large numbers: “If I had a million dollars in investable funds, would I invest that entire amount in Anthropic, even if it trades at well below my assessed value? The answer would be no, given the uncertainties associated with the future of the company, but that answer would change if my portfolio became less concentrated, since its performance would be less a function of any individual company's performance (good or bad),” Damodaran said. In effect, he said he is using the law of large numbers as an ally to not only reduce his risk exposure to individual companies, but also as a basis for making investments in far riskier stocks than he would be otherwise inclined to invest in.Disclaimer: This article has been written by Debaroti Adhikary, who is not a SEBI-registered Research Analyst or an Investment Adviser. articles.title: US: What happens next as Dems take over
articles.summary: Washington: Democrats are preparing a legislative offensive against US President Donald Trump after their sweeping midterm victory handed them control of both chambers of Congress and the power to challenge his policies, investigate his administration and block his nominees.Emboldened by victories deep in traditional Republican territory, the party is promising swift action on living costs and the war in Iran, while signaling that investigations of alleged abuses and corruption will be a major priority.Also read | Did Iran war just blow up in Trump's face?House Democratic leader Hakeem Jeffries, who is in line to become the first Black speaker when the new Congress takes office in January, vowed to go after what he described as "unprecedented corruption" in the government."Because if you have people in high office who are so focused on enriching themselves, their family members, their friends, or their donors, then they're not focused on making life better for the American people," he said.But Democrats will not have a free hand. Trump retains his veto, while Senate rules allow Republicans to obstruct most legislation.Here are the opportunities -- and obstacles -- ahead.First 100 hoursJeffries has promised an ambitious legislative push in the House's first 100 hours, focused on affordability -- the issue that dominated an election shaped by tariffs, high prices and the Iran war.His priorities include restoring expired Affordable Care Act health insurance subsidies, reversing nearly $1 trillion in Medicaid cuts enacted under Trump, rolling back tariffs and pressing for an end to the conflict, which has sent fuel costs soaring.With majorities in both chambers, Democrats can bring their proposals to votes and take charge of spending negotiations. They could use federal budget deadlines to demand concessions, although confrontations over spending risk government shutdowns.'Lawyer up'Oversight may offer an even more immediate means of challenging Trump.Robert Garcia, the Democrat expected to chair the powerful House Oversight Committee, fired off a blunt election-night message to Republicans on social media: "LAWYER UP."Also read | What Trump & Republicans' loss means for IndiaOregon Senator Ron Wyden was even more concise, posting a single word: "Subpoenas."With control of committees in both chambers, Democrats can summon officials, demand documents and hold public hearings, potentially putting Trump and his senior aides under intense scrutiny.Likely subjects include the Trump family's business and cryptocurrency dealings, government contracts involving billionaire Elon Musk, cuts to federal agencies, immigration enforcement and the conduct of the Iran war.Democrats have also signaled interest in the handling of files relating to notorious sex offender Jeffrey Epstein.The administration could resist demands for testimony or documents, triggering court battles.Democrats could pursue Trump's third impeachment, though party leaders have not committed to doing so. The House needs only a simple majority to impeach, but removing a president requires a two-thirds vote in the Senate -- far beyond the party's numbers.Senate muscleThe Senate majority gives Democrats another powerful lever: control of confirmations.They can block Trump's judicial and cabinet nominees, including any selection to fill a Supreme Court vacancy, potentially curbing his influence over the courts long after he leaves office.Also read | Vivek Ramaswamy: Decoding a Republican firebrand's high-decibel fallDemocratic Senate chairs will also decide which bills and investigations receive committee attention.Limits and dealsPassing laws will be much harder than launching investigations.Most legislation must clear a 60-vote hurdle in the Senate to overcome procedural obstruction. Trump can veto bills passed by Congress, and overturning a veto requires two-thirds support in both chambers.He also retains substantial executive powers over immigration, trade and military operations, although lawmakers can seek to constrain them through legislation and spending decisions.Trump struck a conciliatory note after the rout, praising Democrats for doing a "good job" and telling The New York Times that he would accept the result and expected to work with them.He even raised the possibility of cooperation on immigration.But he had previously warned that if Democrats won Congress, "I veto everything" -- a reminder that the next two years could be defined as much by confrontation as compromise.
